findings.title: Do not pipe unverified remote script into sh during build
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh` fetches and executes whatever the remote endpoint returns as root during `docker build`. There is no version pin, checksum, or signature, so the build is non-reproducible and a compromised/tampered endpoint (or DNS/MITM on an unpinned URL) yields arbitrary code execution inside the image. `curl -s` without `-f` also means an HTTP 4xx/5xx error body is silently piped to `sh` instead of failing the build, turning a fetch failure into executing an error page as a script.

findings.title: Do not pipe unverified remote script into shell in image build
findings.whyItBreaks: The new build step fetches https://example.com/install.sh and executes it immediately via `| sh` with no pinning, no checksum/signature verification, and no TLS pinning beyond curl defaults. Any compromise, DNS/TLS MITM, or change of the remote content at build time yields arbitrary code execution with build (and later image runtime) privileges, and the build is not reproducible because the fetched content is mutable. `curl -s` also hides transfer errors and there is no `-f`, so a failed download can silently produce an image missing the intended tooling.

findings.title: Do not pipe an unpinned remote script into sh at build time
findings.whyItBreaks: The added layer downloads https://example.com/install.sh at build time and executes it as root via `| sh` with no version pin, no checksum/signature, and no immutable reference. The bytes executed are whatever the remote endpoint serves at build time, so the image content is non-reproducible and any compromise or change of that endpoint (or a MITM that survives since no integrity check exists) results in arbitrary attacker code embedded in every image built from this Dockerfile. This is a classic unpinned remote-code-execution supply-chain defect, not a stylistic concern.

findings.title: curl download failure is swallowed and build succeeds silently
findings.whyItBreaks: `curl -sL` omits `-f`, so HTTP/network failures do not make curl exit non-zero, and because the command is a pipe (`curl ... | sh`) the RUN layer's exit status comes from `sh`, not curl. If the download fails, `sh` receives empty/error-page input and typically exits 0, so the build reports success while the intended setup never happened — a silently broken image. Failure and the 'legitimate' result are indistinguishable to the build.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault discards ErrMissing, conflating missing key with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) for an absent key and ("", nil) for a key explicitly stored as empty string (src/store.go:7-13). LoadOrDefault drops the error and returns "" in both cases, so callers can no longer distinguish 'key not present' from 'key present with empty value'. The discard is a public/exported contract, so every eventual caller is forced to treat a failed lookup as real data.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault discards ErrMissing, conflating missing key with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: LoadOrDefault is an exported API that ignores the error channel of Load: `v, _ := Load(key, m)` (src/store.go:16) discards ErrMissing (defined at src/store.go:5 and returned at src/store.go:10) and returns the zero value "". A caller therefore cannot distinguish a missing key from a key that is present and legitimately maps to "" — both yield the same string. Any caller that persists, bills, or branches on the value (e.g. writes it to storage or treats empty as a real setting) will silently act on a failed lookup as if it were a real value, whereas Load previously surfaced that failure. This is a public/exported swallow site, so the unusable contract is the defect even though nothing in-repo calls it yet.

findings.title: Run no longer waits for sends; callers may close results too early
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change Run returned only after every `results <- j*2` had been delivered, so `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` was a safe, common pattern. Now Run returns immediately after spawning one goroutine per job (lines 7-9); a caller that closes or reuses `results` right after Run returns races in-flight goroutines that then execute `results <- j*2` on a closed channel, which panics (send on closed channel) or silently drops results. This is an exported function whose observable postcondition (all results delivered before return) was removed.

findings.title: Run no longer waits for sends; completion/ordering contract broken
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change `results <- j*2` executed inline, so Run returned only after all len(jobs) sends had completed, in job order. Now each send happens in a detached goroutine and Run returns immediately without any WaitGroup/join. Any caller that follows the previous semantics breaks: (a) reading/expecting len(jobs) results (or results[jobs[i]] index alignment) after Run returns observes missing or nondeterministically reordered values; (b) the natural `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results)` pattern now panics with `send on closed channel` because the spawned goroutines may send after close; (c) if `results` is unbuffered and the receiver stops reading or Run's caller returns, the goroutines block on send forever and leak (ctx is never consulted on this send path).

findings.title: Run no longer blocks until results are sent; callers can lose results/close early
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change Run sent every result synchronously and only returned after all len(jobs) sends completed, giving callers an implicit completion + backpressure guarantee. Spawning `go func` per job makes Run return immediately while the sends are still pending, so a caller that follows the previous contract (e.g. `Run(ctx, jobs, results); close(results); for v := range results {...}`) now races: late sends hit a closed channel (panic: send on closed channel) or are silently dropped from the drained range, and the delivery order of results is no longer guaranteed. The exported API's blocking semantics changed with no signal to callers.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord OR-logic grants unauthorized record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: Replacing `&&` with `||` turns the conjunctive admin-and-same-tenant requirement into a disjunction, so the guard authorizes deletion if EITHER condition holds. Concretely: (a) any non-admin session whose tenantId matches the record's tenantId now passes (previously rejected), letting an ordinary user delete any record in their tenant, including records owned by others (RecordRef.ownerId is ignored); (b) any session with isAdmin=true now passes regardless of record.tenantId, allowing cross-tenant admin deletion (previously rejected). Both are authorization bypasses with data-loss impact, and this is an exported public predicate whose contract is the defect even without in-repo callers.

findings.title: Authorization bypass in canDeleteRecord (&& changed to ||)
findings.whyItBreaks: The delete-authorization predicate changed from conjunction to disjunction. Previously a caller could delete only when the session was an admin AND tenant-matched. Now `session.isAdmin || session.tenantId === record.tenantId` returns true in two illegitimate cases: (1) any non-admin user whose tenantId equals the record's tenantId can delete arbitrary records in their tenant (privilege escalation past the admin requirement); (2) any admin of tenant A can delete records belonging to tenant B (cross-tenant isolation break) because the tenant-equality check is short-circuited away whenever isAdmin is true. This is an exported authorization API, so every eventual caller inherits the broken contract even though no in-repo caller exists yet.

findings.title: Loosen canDeleteRecord from AND to OR breaks tenant/admin authorization
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate previously required BOTH admin status AND matching tenant (session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId). Swapping to || makes it true when EITHER holds, so (a) any admin of any tenant can now delete records belonging to other tenants (cross-tenant deletion, session.isAdmin=true regardless of tenantId), and (b) any non-admin whose tenantId matches the record's tenantId can delete it (admin requirement entirely removed — every user in a tenant gains delete rights over all that tenant's records). This is a direct authorization bypass on the delete capability.

findings.title: clampPercent name promises clamping its body never does
findings.whyItBreaks: The PR renames the exported `toPercent` to `clampPercent` (src/progress.ts:1), promising the result is capped to [0,100], but the unchanged body at src/progress.ts:2 computes `Math.round((done/total)*100)` with no bound. Callers now trust a cap that does not exist: `progressBar` feeds `pct` straight into string replication (src/progress.ts:7), so `progressBar(5, 4)` yields pct=125 and `"-".repeat(100 - 125)` throws `RangeError: Invalid count value: -25`; `progressBar(-1, 4)` throws on `"#".repeat(-25)`; `progressBar(1, 0)` yields Infinity and throws on `repeat(Infinity)`. A public carrier whose promised capping affects the value callers receive is a contract defect regardless of whether external consumers exist yet.

findings.title: clampPercent promises clamping but returns unbounded values
findings.whyItBreaks: The renamed carrier `clampPercent` promises a clamped value in [0,100], but the unchanged body `Math.round((done / total) * 100)` @src/progress.ts:2 clamps nothing: for done > total it returns >100 (e.g. clampPercent(150,100) = 150) and for negative done it returns a negative number. The relying caller `progressBar` feeds that value straight into string repeat: `"-".repeat(100 - pct)` @src/progress.ts:7 with pct>100 becomes `"-".repeat(negative)` and throws RangeError: Invalid count value, and `"#".repeat(pct)` @src/progress.ts:7 throws for a negative pct. So the new name asserts a guarantee (positive/bounded) that the implementation does not provide, and the caller trusts it.

findings.title: clampPercent name promises capping but body never clamps
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff renames the exported symbol toPercent -> clampPercent, so the public contract now promises a percent capped to [0,100]. The body is unchanged: Math.round((done / total) * 100) with no clamp, so clampPercent(150, 100) returns 150 and clampPercent(-10, 100) returns -10. Any caller trusting the new name for a bounded value receives an out-of-range number; the internal consumer progressBar feeds that value straight into "#".repeat(pct)/"-".repeat(100 - pct) at src/progress.ts:6, which throws RangeError for pct < 0 or > 100. The rename also removes the old exported name toPercent, breaking any external importer, without an alias.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows errors and updateFontSize persists defaults, losing settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change a malformed or type-invalid raw value threw out of parseSettings, so updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:19) aborted before calling save. Now the catch returns `{ ...DEFAULTS }`, which is indistinguishable from a legitimate parse result, so updateFontSize overwrites the stored file (src/settings.ts:22) with theme="light", fontSize=size. Concretely, a stored value like `{"theme":"dark","fontSize":"x"}` previously raised "bad fontSize" and wrote nothing; it now silently discards the user's theme and writes back defaults. The public exported `parseSettings` (src/settings.ts:8) also no longer lets any caller distinguish failure from a real result.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows errors, silently resetting settings to defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch-all converts every failure (invalid JSON, missing/wrong-typed theme or fontSize) into a default object. Previously the thrown Error propagated out of parseSettings. Its caller updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20) does `const settings = parseSettings(raw)`, mutates fontSize, and unconditionally `save(...)`. With the swallow, corrupt/incomplete stored settings (e.g. a valid JSON object that has a custom theme but is missing fontSize) no longer abort the update: theme is silently reset to "light" and the defaults are written back to storage, discarding the user's existing value. The failure and the legitimate-defaults value are indistinguishable to any caller.

findings.title: Don't swallow parseSettings errors; updateFontSize persists defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, parseSettings propagated JSON.parse failures and its `bad theme`/`bad fontSize` validation errors. The added try/catch returns `{ ...DEFAULTS }` for every failure, so callers can no longer distinguish 'corrupt/invalid settings' from a legitimate choice of defaults. On the live in-repo path this is destructive: updateFontSize (src/settings.ts:20) calls parseSettings(raw), then unconditionally sets fontSize and calls save(JSON.stringify(settings)) at src/settings.ts:22. With the swallow, a malformed/legacy raw string no longer aborts the update — it silently yields theme='light', the caller mutates fontSize, and it persists `{"theme":"light","fontSize":<size>}`, permanently discarding the user's actual theme (and any other stored fields) instead of surfacing the error and leaving the stored settings untouched. The exported function is a public contract too: every caller is now forced to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: Report misattributes artifacts: uses "verified" ref but reports branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport() previously returned the pair { builtFrom: commit, artifacts: artifactsAt(commit) }, so report.builtFrom always identified the commit the artifacts came from. The change keeps builtFrom as the branch commit (build.ref(branch)) but now fetches artifacts with build.artifactsAt(build.ref("verified")). Whenever the "verified" ref resolves to a different commit than the branch ref, the returned BuildReport pairs a commit with artifact lists that were not produced from it — every consumer reading report.builtFrom to key/label/validate report.artifacts gets silently wrong provenance (mislabeled build, wrong artifact set attributed to the branch).

findings.title: buildReport pairs branch commit with artifacts from a different ref
findings.whyItBreaks: Changed line 13-14 replaces the resolved branch commit with build.ref("verified") as the key passed to build.artifactsAt, while builtFrom on line 14 still uses the branch commit. When ref("verified") resolves to anything other than ref(branch) (the normal case for any non-verified branch, and the entire reason a build system carries a distinct 'verified' ref), the BuildReport returns artifacts from commit B but labels them builtFrom = commit A. Consumers that pair builtFrom with artifacts (attribution, provenance, display) now report the wrong commit for those artifacts, and the branch argument no longer governs which artifacts are returned. `verified` is also computed but builtFrom ignores it, so the two report fields are internally inconsistent.

findings.title: Artifacts pulled from unrelated 'verified' ref, report mixes refs
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change both `builtFrom` and `artifacts` were derived from the same ref (`build.ref(branch)`, base line 12/14), so a report described one build. Now `builtFrom` still reports the branch commit while `artifacts` come from a hardcoded `build.ref("verified")` (line 13). Any consumer rendering the report attributes artifacts to a commit they were not built from, and the "verified" ref is neither derived from `branch` nor validated to exist for the given build, so the lookup silently feeds whatever `ref`/`artifactsAt` produce for a missing ref into a public, externally consumed structure.

findings.title: recentEntries no longer caps results to limit
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc contract at line 1 promises 'at most limit entries', and the base implemented it with slice(0, limit). The new body only special-cases limit<=0, then returns the full reversed array, dropping the slice entirely. For the live caller renderFeed (line 9), recentEntries(all, 20) now returns all(a) entries: any feed with more than 20 items returns page.length>20, and the fixed-size buffer loop at line 11 writes out[20], out[21]... against `new Array<string>(20)` (line 10), extending the array with trailing undefined holes and yielding an oversized, corrupted feed instead of the newest 20.

findings.title: Restore limit truncation in recentEntries
findings.whyItBreaks: The change reverses all input and then returns it unconditionally for any limit > 0, deleting the previous `.slice(0, limit)`. The doc contract (line 1) still promises "at most `limit` entries", and renderFeed (line 9) passes limit 20 and writes into a preallocated `new Array<string>(20)`. With 21+ entries, page.length > 20, so line 11 writes out[20], out[21], ... growing the array past 20 instead of returning a 20-entry page. The cap is silently removed for every limit value.

findings.title: Restore slice(0, limit); recentEntries now ignores limit
findings.whyItBreaks: The refactor removed the `.slice(0, limit)` call, so for every positive `limit` the function returns the entire reversed array instead of at most `limit` entries, contradicting its own doc contract. The in-repo consumer `renderFeed` (src/feed.ts:9) calls `recentEntries(all, 20)` and relies on the cap: it allocates `const out = new Array<string>(20)` and loops `i < page.length`, so when `all.length > 20` it writes past index 20, extending `out`, and returns all entries instead of the newest 20.

findings.title: Update entry-count header to match filtered rows
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 20 now drops stale entries from `rows`, but the header at line 22 still computes `# entry-count: ${entries.length}` from the full input array. Any manifest containing at least one `stale: true` entry is emitted with an entry-count larger than the number of data rows it actually contains (e.g. 2 entries, 1 stale -> header says 2, body lists 1). `renderManifest` is the exported public producer of the manifest string, so the count/metadata contract that callers read no longer describes the payload they receive.

findings.title: Keep entry-count consistent with filtered manifest rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff filters stale entries out of the emitted rows (line 20-21) but the `# entry-count:` header still receives `entries.length` (line 22), which includes stale entries. A consumer that trusts the declared count to size, index, or validate the row list will see a count that overstates the rows actually present whenever any entry is stale; before this change the count and row count always agreed.

findings.title: Fix entry-count header to match filtered rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The change filters out stale entries into `live` and emits rows from `live`, but line 22 still passes `entries.length` to `headerLines`, so `# entry-count: N` counts all entries (including stale ones) while only `live.length` rows are actually emitted. Before this change the header count always equaled the number of rows, so the manifest was self-consistent. Now any consumer that validates the header against the parsed rows, sizes a buffer/preallocation from the count, or checks completeness (e.g. "did I receive all N entries?") sees an inflated count and a mismatch whenever any entry is stale. The exported `renderManifest` output contract is silently broken.

findings.title: Restore execute(): it now always throws and cannot return a value
findings.whyItBreaks: `execute` is exported with signature `(input: string) => string`, but its body was replaced with `throw new Error("always fails")`. Every call to this public entry point now aborts unconditionally instead of returning a value, so any caller that depends on its result breaks (previous behavior returned `input.toUpperCase()`). This is the module's only exported symbol, so the whole file's contract is now unusable.

findings.title: Restore execute(): it now unconditionally throws instead of returning

The function is declared `execute(input: string): string`, so callers expect a string back; now every invocation raises instead, so no caller can ever receive a value. This is a total loss of the module's only behavior and breaks the public contract (a function whose signature promises a `string` never returns one). No in-repo callers exist, but this is an exported public API, so the unusable contract ships as-is to all external consumers.

findings.title: Restore execute() return; it now throws on every call
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported `execute(input: string): string` previously returned `input.toUpperCase()`. The change replaces the only body statement with `throw new Error("always fails")`, so every invocation now aborts with an exception instead of returning a string. This is an unconditional failure of the function's sole advertised behavior and of its `: string` return contract — no input can produce a value, so the core path is unusable for all callers.

findings.title: Viewer guard in isEligible over-blocks the read-only action path
findings.whyItBreaks: isEligible() now returns false for any viewer, but the sole caller handle() has a distinct, legitimate viewer action: it returns "read-only" for viewers at src/handler.ts:25. Because handle() checks `if (!isEligible(req)) return "rejected";` first (src/handler.ts:24), every viewer with status==="active" and attempts < MAX_ATTEMPTS — previously admitted and served the read-only path — is now rejected before reaching it. The read-only action is the whole point of admitting viewers, so the guard rejects an action it should not govern, and line 25 is now dead code.

findings.title: Viewer gate makes read-only action unreachable, rejects valid viewers
findings.whyItBreaks: Substituting req={status:"active",role:"viewer",attempts:0}: pre-change isEligible returned true and handle() (src/handler.ts:25) returned "read-only"; post-change the new `if (req.role === "viewer") return false;` makes isEligible false, so handle() returns "rejected" at src/handler.ts:24. The read-only path at src/handler.ts:25 is now dead code, and viewers with valid status/attempts lose legitimate read-only access.

findings.title: isEligible rejects viewers, making handle's read-only path unreachable
findings.whyItBreaks: The new guard `if (req.role === "viewer") return false;` (src/handler.ts:18) makes isEligible false for any viewer. In handle (src/handler.ts:23), `if (!isEligible(req)) return "rejected";` fires first (line 24), so an active viewer with attempts < MAX_ATTEMPTS — which previously returned "read-only" via line 25 — now returns "rejected". The viewer branch at src/handler.ts:25 is now dead code, evidencing that viewers were intended to be eligible for their own read-only outcome. The changed predicate governs "eligibility for processing" but is now also rejecting the distinct read-only action it should not govern, i.e. over-blocking a legitimately approvable request.

findings.title: Payment gate on shared canProceed blocks saving unpaid drafts
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is a shared predicate read by two distinct actions. src/actions.ts:4 submitOrder is legitimately governed by payment, but src/actions.ts:9 saveDraft also calls canProceed and now returns "blocked" whenever payment === "missing". Saving a draft is legitimately approvable independent of payment, so this rejects a valid action: saveDraft({state:"draft",payment:"missing"}) previously returned "saved", now returns "blocked". The change only needed to tighten the submit path, but it tightens both.

findings.title: saveDraft now blocked unless payment is paid
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is a shared predicate read by two distinct actions. Substituting the new value payment="missing" against the added guard `order.payment === "paid"` (src/policy.ts:7) makes canProceed return false for a draft order, so saveDraft returns "blocked" (src/actions.ts:9) instead of "saved". Saving a draft does not depend on payment, so the payment predicate must not govern it; before this change saveDraft returned "saved" for state="draft", payment="missing". submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) is legitimately gated by payment, so only the saveDraft call-site regresses.

findings.title: Payment gate on shared canProceed breaks saving unpaid drafts
findings.whyItBreaks: canProceed is a single shared predicate read by two distinct actions. saveDraft (src/actions.ts:9) gates the 'save a draft' action on it, but a draft is by definition not yet paid (`payment` is "missing" until paid), so the added clause `order.payment === "paid"` is false for any normal draft, canProceed returns false, and saveDraft returns "blocked" instead of "saved". The payment precondition the PR intends legitimately governs submitOrder (src/actions.ts:4) but NOT saving a draft, so the change rejects a legitimately-approvable action.

findings.title: publishSnapshot pairs channel commit with stable's files
findings.whyItBreaks: The new `stable = repo.headCommit("stable")` (line 14) is fed into `files: repo.filesAt(stable)` (line 18), while the returned `commit` is still `head = repo.headCommit(channel)` (line 13, line 16). The Snapshot contract (commit/channel/files, lines 6-10) implies the file list belongs to the reported commit+channel; after this change every snapshot for a channel other than "stable" reports files from the stable branch, so consumers persisting or publishing the snapshot attach the wrong file set to the wrong commit. Additionally, repos/channels with no "stable" ref now make `headCommit("stable")` throw where the previous code only touched the caller's channel.

findings.title: publishSnapshot lists stable's files under the channel's commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The returned Snapshot is self-inconsistent: `commit` is the commit returned by `repo.headCommit(channel)` (line 13/16), but `files` is now produced by `repo.filesAt(stable)` where `stable = repo.headCommit("stable")` (lines 14/18). Before this diff, `files` used `repo.filesAt(head)`, so the file list matched the reported commit. Any consumer that trusts `snapshot.commit` to describe `snapshot.files` (e.g. publishing a manifest, diffing, or fetching blobs by commit) will now associate the channel's commit id with a different ref's file listing, and `channel` in the snapshot no longer corresponds to the listed files either. The change silently rewrites the meaning of an existing exported result rather than adding a new field.

findings.title: publishSnapshot returns files from "stable" but commit from the requested channel
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change files came from repo.filesAt(head), where head = repo.headCommit(channel), so a Snapshot's files always corresponded to its own commit/channel. The new line 14 fetches an unrelated hardcoded ref (repo.headCommit("stable")) and line 18 uses that to populate files, while commit (line 16) and channel (line 17) still describe the requested channel. Any consumer that pairs snapshot.commit with snapshot.files now reads a file listing from a different commit than advertised (wrong content, silently not an error), and publishing a non-"stable" channel is misrepresented. If the repo has no "stable" ref, headCommit("stable") also yields an invalid/undefined commit for filesAt, breaking the call for every channel.

findings.title: Honor or remove the ignored `limit` parameter in build()
findings.whyItBreaks: `build` now advertises a `limit` cap (`def build(prefix, limit=10)`) but the body still uses the hardcoded `max_count = 10` and never reads `limit`. Every caller that passes `limit` (e.g. `build('x', limit=3)`) receives 10 items instead of 3 — an externally observable, silently wrong result with no error. Because this is a public module-level function, the signature itself is the contract; a capping promise the body does not implement is a defect even before any in-repo caller exists.

findings.title: build() ignores new limit param, always returns 10 items
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature now advertises a caller-controlled size via `limit`, but the body still computes `max_count = 10` and loops `range(max_count)`, so the parameter is never read. Any caller passing `build(prefix, limit=3)` (or any non-default) still receives exactly 10 elements, silently violating the cap the parameter promises; a caller sizing downstream storage or paging on `limit` gets an over-long result. findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC comparison in webhook verify()

findings.title: Do not echo secret TOKEN into CI logs
findings.whyItBreaks: The added step maps the repository/deploy credential `secrets.TOKEN` into the environment and expands it with `echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`, writing the secret's value to the job log. The step also runs before `make build`, so the exposure is unconditional on every push (workflow triggers on `on: push`).

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer so large git diffs do not abort the review
findings.whyItBreaks: `spawnSync` defaults `maxBuffer` to 1024*1024 (1 MiB). The only option now passed is `{ cwd, encoding }`. On line 140 the full patch is captured via `git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha], cwd)`; for a PR whose diff exceeds 1 MiB, Node kills the child, sets `res.error` (ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER/ENOBUFS) and leaves `res.status` null. `res.status !== 0` then throws `git diff ... failed:` with empty `stderr` (res.error is never inspected), so `runGithub`'s catch posts 'Needlefish: review failed' and sets exitCode 1 — every large PR is rejected without an actual review. Previously the 64 MiB buffer (still used by the sibling gh helpers at lines 19 and 29) allowed these diffs.

findings.title: Keep bundle.baseSha as the merge base, not the PR base tip
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 138 computes baseSha = PR_BASE_SHA || merge-base(origin/main, HEAD) and line 139 computes the true diff base mergeBase = merge-base(baseSha, headSha). The patch (line 140) and changedFiles (line 141) are both diffed from mergeBase, but the bundle now advertises baseSha. Whenever PR_BASE_SHA is the base-branch tip rather than the fork point (the normal GitHub case once the base branch has advanced), baseSha != mergeBase, so the bundle handed to the model and the serialized/rendered result report a base that does not match the diff; any consumer reading the base tree at baseSha sees base-branch commits that are not part of the PR. Canonical needlefish semantics require the merge base here (schema comment: 'baseSha, which is the merge base'; local.test.ts asserts result.baseSha == mergeBase and prBaseSha != baseSha), with the base tip carried separately.

findings.title: Restore spawnSync maxBuffer for the git() helper
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer makes git() use spawnSync's default 1 MiB stdout/stderr cap. Line 140 runs `git diff mergeBase headSha` for the entire PR; any PR whose diff exceeds 1 MiB (lockfiles, generated/minified/vendored files) makes spawnSync abort with ENOBUFS, res.status becomes null, and line 38-39 throws. That git() call sits before the try/catch at line 176, so the throw escapes runGithub and no 'review failed' check is posted. The base revision kept a 64 MiB buffer, and gh()/ghText() still use 64 MiB, so this is an inconsistent regression.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git() or large PRs fail with ENOBUFS
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1 MiB. git() is used at src/adapters/github.ts:140 to run `git diff mergeBase headSha`, i.e. the entire PR patch, and a diff over ~1 MiB (lockfiles, snapshots, generated/dist files) now exceeds the default. Verified on node v24.15.0: a 2 MiB stdout spawnSync returns status=null, signal=SIGTERM, error.code=ENOBUFS, stdout truncated to 1114112 bytes. Because the guard at line 38 only checks `res.status !== 0` (null !== 0 is true) and ignores res.error, it throws `git diff <base> <head> failed: ` with an empty stderr. This aborts runGithub for large PRs that previously worked with the 64 MiB buffer, and since these bundle-assembly calls (lines 137-141) run before the try/catch at line 176, the `postCheck('review failed')` fallback is bypassed and no Needlefish check-run is posted at all.

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox on codex exec invocation
findings.whyItBreaks: The `-s read-only` flag was the only thing pinning the sandbox for the spawned `codex exec`. With no `-s` arg, codex resolves the sandbox from config: `codex-rs/exec/src/lib.rs:328-332` maps the absent flag to `None`, and thread start then uses `sandbox_mode_from_permission_profile(&config.permissions.effective_permission_profile(), ...)` (lib.rs:1363-1376). Read-only is only the *default* when the user has not configured anything; a user with `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"`, `"danger-full-access"`, or a `[permissions]` profile now runs this reviewer (which feeds untrusted PR content to the agent) with write/exec capability instead of the previously guaranteed read-only. That is exactly the untrusted-code execution surface the read-only flag existed to prevent, and it changes silently for users whose own config is not read-only.

findings.title: Restore read-only sandbox for the codex exec review subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` deletes the only hard guarantee that the spawned `codex exec` runs model-generated shell commands without repo write access. Codex resolves the sandbox as `sandbox_mode_override.or(config.sandbox_mode)` (CLI flag wins), and when no flag is passed it falls back to the user's config.toml `sandbox_mode` or, for a trusted working directory, `workspace-write`. Headless `codex exec` also forces `approval_policy = never`, so escalating commands are auto-executed with no prompt. With cwd = the reviewed repo, an operator whose config sets `sandbox_mode = "workspace-write"` (the documented default recommendation for coding) or `danger-full-access` now lets the review agent modify the repository under review or run write-capable commands off untrusted PR content — behavior the base revision made impossible. The function returns a final message file and needs no write access, so the flag was pure safety with no functional cost.

findings.title: Removing '-s read-only' lets the reviewer write to the reviewed repo
findings.whyItBreaks: `runCodex` now spawns `codex exec` with no explicit sandbox, whereas base forced `-s read-only`. In the installed codex (0.159.3) `-s/--sandbox` is optional and has no default (exec/src/cli.rs maps it to `None`), so the effective sandbox comes from config: `derive_permission_profile` (codex-rs/config/src/config_toml.rs:819-828 @ rust-v0.159.3) resolves `None` to `SandboxMode::WorkspaceWrite` for any project that has a recorded trust decision. This environment's `$CODEX_HOME/config.toml` contains `[projects."/tmp/needlefish-managed-tQ7CBR/runner-repo"] trust_level = "trusted"`, and `runCodex` sets `cwd: opts.repoPath`, so the spawned agent (whose prompt is driven by untrusted PR content) can now run model-generated shell commands with write access to the repository under review. Previously the explicit flag pinned read-only regardless of ambient trust config, so the change also makes sandbox behavior machine-dependent.

findings.title: Restore merge-base before diffing; two-dot diff leaks base-branch changes
findings.whyItBreaks: `git diff baseSha HEAD` is a two-dot (tree-to-tree) diff. When `PR_BASE_SHA` points at the current base-branch tip (the usual GitHub payload value) and the base branch has moved on since this PR branched, `baseSha` is NOT an ancestor of HEAD, so the diff contains every base-branch commit as a reverse change in addition to the PR's own changes. The previous code anchored on `git merge-base baseSha headSha` and diffed `mergeBase..headSha`, which is exactly the PR's patch. Consequences: (1) the prompt patch shown to the reviewer is polluted with unrelated changes, and (2) `changedFileSet` classifies those extra files, so `changedPaths` (used by `inlineComments` to allow inline comments) now includes files this PR never touched, enabling findings to be posted against unrelated files, and (3) any surface/security classification derived from `changedFiles` is skewed. Behavior is identical only in the narrow case where baseSha is already the merge base or an ancestor of HEAD.

findings.title: Restore merge-base before diffing; base tip diff pulls in unrelated commits
findings.whyItBreaks: In the Actions path baseSha comes from PR_BASE_SHA (the base branch tip) while HEAD/headSha is the PR commit. Previously the code diffed `merge-base(baseSha, headSha)..headSha`, i.e. only the PR's own commits (src/adapters/github.ts:138 in the base revision). Now it diffs `baseSha..HEAD`, so whenever the base branch advanced past the branch point the patch contains the base-only commits rendered in reverse (their changes appear as deletions attributed to this PR) and `changedFileSet(cwd, baseSha)` returns files the PR never touched. Those extra paths flow into `bundle.changedFiles` (surface mis-classification, wrong `focus`/verdict basis) and into `changedPaths`, which the `inlineComments` filter `changedPaths.has(f.file)` @src/adapters/github.ts:62 uses to decide which findings get posted as inline review comments — anchoring comments to files/lines outside the PR diff. The literal `"HEAD"` also replaces the previously used `headSha`, so the patch no longer tracks the SHA that is posted as `commit_id`/`head_sha`, adding to the divergence when HEAD is a merge ref.

findings.title: Restore merge-base normalization: two-dot diff reviews base-branch changes
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change the patch was `git diff merge-base(baseSha, headSha) headSha` and the changed-file set was derived from the same merge base. The new code drops the merge-base step and diffs `baseSha..HEAD` directly. `PR_BASE_SHA` is the base branch tip (the `|| git merge-base origin/main HEAD` fallback at line 138 exists precisely to synthesize a merge base when that tip is absent), so whenever the base branch has moved past the PR's fork point, the two-dot diff includes base-only commits as reversals and the changed-file set becomes a superset/subset of the PR's real files. Consequences: (1) the LLM reviews unrelated base-branch content and can emit bogus findings the author must triage; (2) `changedPaths` (line 141) now contains files the PR never touched, so `inlineComments`' `changedPaths.has(f.file)` filter (line 63) admits them and `postReview` sends review comments for paths/lines outside the PR diff, which GitHub rejects with 422; the `catch` in `postReview` then silently downgrades to a body-only review, dropping every inline comment. The reverse case (base changed a file the PR also changed to the same content) silently omits PR files from `changedPaths`, so their findings are never posted inline.

findings.title: Removing replacer functions lets $-patterns corrupt injected bundle/patch
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace only skips $-substitution when the replacement argument is a function. Passing a plain string (JSON.stringify(bundle,null,2) at line 25, JSON.stringify(candidate,null,2) at line 32, bundle.patch at line 33) makes the engine interpret $$, $&, $`, $' (and, for a group-less search string, literal $1..$99) inside the payload. bundle.patch is raw diff text and routinely contains these sequences (shell $$/PID, JS/regex replace snippets, template strings), and bundle JSON embeds that same patch, so the BEGIN/END DIFF and code context delivered to review.md/critic.md get silently rewritten — e.g. a patch line containing $& is replaced with the literal search token {{PATCH}}/{{BUNDLE}}, and $$ collapses to $. The models then review altered content, so findings/verdicts can be produced against text that does not match the real diff. The base revision deliberately used () => ... thunks to avoid exactly this; this diff reverts that protection.

findings.title: Keep function-form replace args to avoid $ pattern substitution
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace only skips replacement-pattern processing when the second argument is a function; a string argument interprets `$$`, `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'`, `$n`, `$<name>`. The injected values are arbitrary repo-derived text: `JSON.stringify(bundle, null, 2)` (includes bundle.patch and file content), `JSON.stringify(candidate, null, 2)`, and `bundle.patch`. Any occurrence of `$&` becomes the literal `{{BUNDLE}}`/`{{FINDINGS}}`/`{{PATCH}}` token, `$$` collapses to `$`, `` $` `` expands to all template text before the match, and `$'` expands to all text after it. These sequences are common in shell scripts (`$$`, `$'\t'`), sed/awk/regex-replacement code (`$&`, `$1`), and Makefiles, so the prompts sent to the model can be silently truncated, duplicated, or corrupted. The base revision deliberately used `() => ...` to prevent exactly this, so the change reintroduces a fixed defect.

findings.title: String replacement re-enables $-pattern substitution, corrupting prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: When the second argument to String.prototype.replace is a STRING, the JS engine interprets special replacement patterns in it: $$ -> $, $& -> the matched substring (here literally "{{BUNDLE}}"/"{{FINDINGS}}"/"{{PATCH}}"), $` -> the ENTIRE portion of the prompt before the match, and $' -> the entire portion after the match. Only a FUNCTION replacement suppresses this interpretation, which is exactly what the previous `() => JSON.stringify(...)` / `() => bundle.patch` form did. The injected content is arbitrary: `JSON.stringify(bundle, null, 2)` and `JSON.stringify(candidate, null, 2)` leave `$` unescaped, and `bundle.patch` is a raw unified diff that routinely contains `$` sequences (template literals, `$VAR`, regex/replacement literals like `$&`, `$$`). Any injected text containing `$&`, `$$`, `` $` ``, or `$'` is silently rewritten before being sent to the model. The worst case is `` $` `` / `$'`, which splices the surrounding prompt text (including the whole prior prompt body) into the position, massively corrupting -- and enabling prompt-injection amplification of -- the review/critic prompt. This is a regression introduced by this diff: base used the function form and was immune.

findings.title: Pin fallback review to reviewed commit instead of PR head
findings.whyItBreaks: postReview's primary call pins the review with `commit_id: headSha` (src/adapters/github.ts:89), but the diff drops `` `commit_id=${headSha}` `` from the catch/fallback `gh api` call. Per the GitHub REST docs for 'Create a review for a pull request', commit_id 'Defaults to the most recent commit in the pull request when you do not specify a value.' So when the primary post fails and the fallback runs, the review (including REQUEST_CHANGES, which the caller derives from the failing verdict at line 183-184) is recorded against the PR's current head rather than the SHA Needlefish actually reviewed. If a commit lands between checkout/review and posting, the review gate is attached to a commit that was never examined.

findings.title: normalizeFinding swallows malformed input into fake P1 findings
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change normalizeFinding threw on every failure: non-object input, invalid severity, invalid category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, and non-finite or <=0 lineStart/lineEnd. normalizeReview then either surfaced that error (strict) or dropped the bad finding (non-strict). Head replaces all of it with failure-as-value: invalid/absent severity → "P1", invalid category → "bug", missing file → "", missing title → "Untitled finding", missing whyItBreaks/suggestedFix → "", lineStart → 0 and lineEnd → Number(raw.lineEnd ?? raw.lineStart ?? 0) (NaN for a non-numeric lineEnd, since the finite/positive checks are gone). normalizeReview now stores these coerced objects unconditionally at src/shared/schema.ts:131, so callers can no longer tell "model produced a broken finding" from "model produced a real P1 bug". A consumer that counts findings or derives the verdict from severity will treat failed output as a legitimate high-severity finding (e.g. flip pass → changes_requested) and persist it.

findings.title: Stop discarding malformed-finding errors via silent defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: The old normalizeFinding threw on any malformed finding (invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, non-positive lineStart/lineEnd), and normalizeReview(raw, strict=false) dropped entries that failed this validation. The new body instead maps every failure to a default: invalid severity → "P1" (src/shared/schema.ts:98), invalid category → "bug" (:100-102), missing file → "" (:103), missing/zero lineStart → 0 (:104), lineEnd → 0 (:105). Failure is therefore indistinguishable from a real finding: e.g. normalizeFinding({}) now yields a fabricated P1 bug finding with file "" at line 0 rather than signalling an error, and a severity typo (e.g. "CRITICAL" intended as P0) is silently downgraded to P1. Callers can no longer tell "the model produced unusable output" from "the model produced a legitimate P1", so a parse failure gets emitted as a real finding anchored to an invalid line.

findings.title: normalizeFinding swallows malformed input and fabricates a P1 finding
findings.whyItBreaks: The old body threw on every malformed field (not an object, invalid severity/category, empty file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, non-positive lineStart/lineEnd); those throws propagated out of normalizeReview (default strict=true) so callers could reject an unusable model response. The new body returns a Finding for anything: an unknown severity is silently rewritten to "P1", an unknown/missing category to "bug", a missing title to "Untitled finding", a missing file to "", and a missing/invalid lineStart to 0. A caller can no longer distinguish "model produced a valid review" from "model produced garbage", and the garbage is surfaced as a real P1 finding with a line anchor of 0 that points at no change (violating the "must cite a concrete changed file and line range" contract downstream). This is an exported public function, so every eventual caller is forced to conflate failure with a legitimate value.

findings.title: normalizeReview drops the `strict` parameter, breaking lenient and strict callers
findings.whyItBreaks: The public signature changed from normalizeReview(raw, strict = true) to normalizeReview(raw). Callers that passed strict=false for the lenient path previously got malformed findings filtered out (try/catch -> null -> filtered); they now receive coerced, defaulted findings injected into the review. Callers relying on the default strict=true path previously got a thrown error when the model emitted a malformed finding; they now get a silently "successful" review containing fabricated entries. Typed callers passing a second argument no longer compile. Both existing modes change observable output.

findings.title: Restore explicit repo for gh pr view in pre-checkout step
findings.whyItBreaks: The `Resolve PR refs` step runs BEFORE `Checkout PR head` (line 42), so on a clean self-hosted workspace there is no git repo/remote yet. `gh pr view` without `-R`/`GH_REPO` cannot resolve the repository: verified locally that with GH_TOKEN set and GITHUB_REPOSITORY=foo/bar, `gh pr view 123 --json headRefOid` in a non-git dir fails with 'failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository'; gh only honors GH_REPO (gh help environment) and never GITHUB_REPOSITORY. The removed `REPO: ${{ github.repository }}` env var was the only source of repo context. This path is only reached on workflow_dispatch (on pull_request, EVENT_HEAD is non-empty so the else branch is skipped), so manual triggers of the review bot fail. Amplifier: with the default `bash -e` shell the failing command substitution in `echo "$(...)"` does NOT abort (verified: `bash -e -c 'echo "h=$(false)"; echo reached'` exits 0), so the step can silently write empty `head=`/`base=` outputs instead of failing loudly; the checkout then falls back to the default ref and the review runs with empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA.

findings.title: Restore repo arg for `gh pr view` in pre-checkout refs step
findings.whyItBreaks: These two `gh pr view` calls execute in the `Resolve PR refs` step, which runs BEFORE `actions/checkout` (line 42). With `-R "$REPO"` removed and no `GH_REPO` set, gh must resolve the repo from a git remote in the CWD; `$GITHUB_WORKSPACE` has no .git at this point. gh does not read Actions' `GITHUB_REPOSITORY` (the 2.98.0 binary contains zero occurrences of that literal), so it fails at repo resolution. The `else` branch is exactly the workflow_dispatch path (`EVENT_HEAD` empty for a manual trigger), so manual runs now die with `failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository (or any of the parent directories): .git` / `a repository is required; re-run in a repository or supply one with --repo owner/name`, and `steps.refs.outputs.head/base` are never produced. If a self-hosted runner happens to leave a stale .git in the workspace, gh may instead silently resolve the WRONG repository and fetch wrong SHAs.

findings.title: Removing -R/REPO breaks gh pr view on manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: The `else` branch only runs for `workflow_dispatch` (EVENT_HEAD `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` is empty). `gh` resolves a repository from `--repo`/`-R`, the `GH_REPO` env var, or a git remote in the cwd — it does NOT read `GITHUB_REPOSITORY`, and the `REPO` env var removed here was the only thing supplying it. This step (`id: refs`) runs BEFORE `actions/checkout` @.github/workflows/review.yml:42, so the workspace has no git repo/remote yet, and `gh pr view` exits non-zero with 'a repository is required; re-run in a repository or supply one with --repo owner/name'. Because the call is a command substitution inside `echo`, the non-zero exit is discarded: the step still exits 0 and writes empty `head=`/`base=` to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`, so `steps.refs.outputs.head`/`base` are blank and the subsequent checkout/review run against the wrong (default-branch/empty) refs instead of the requested PR.

findings.title: normalizeReview silently swallows malformed output as empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes all five `throw new Error("malformed review output: ...")` guards (base src/shared/schema.ts:115-131) and replaces them with `raw?.x ?? default` coercions. A non-object, missing/non-string summary, or non-array findings/checked/residual_risks now returns `{summary:"", findings:[], checked:[], residual_risks:[]}` instead of surfacing a failure. Because `findings: []` is byte-identical to a legitimately clean review, every caller is forced to conflate "the model returned garbage" with "the model reviewed and found nothing" — the classic failure-as-value hazard, and in a PR-gate context an empty findings list is exactly the shape that maps to PASS. normalizeReview is exported (src/shared/schema.ts:114), so the unusable contract ships now even though this repo has no in-repo callers.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed review output as empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed guards threw on non-object input, non-string summary, and non-array findings/checked/residual_risks. The new body substitutes empty defaults for every one of those failure cases (`summary: ""`, `findings: []`, `checked: []`, `residual_risks: []`). An exported caller (this is a public module surface) can no longer distinguish 'model returned garbage/truncated output' from a legitimate review that genuinely found zero issues and wrote an empty summary. Downstream that conflates parse failure with a clean result — a failed review is now persisted/reported as an empty (passing) review instead of aborting or retrying.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed-output errors as empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version threw on every malformed shape (non-object, non-string summary, non-array findings/checked/residual_risks), which is the only failure signal this exported parser produced. The head version replaces all five guards with `Array.isArray(...) ? ... : []` and `String(raw?.summary ?? "")`, so `null`, `{}`, truncated JSON, or an object with `findings` mis-shaped now normalize to a fully-formed RawReview with empty summary, zero findings, zero checked, zero residual risks. Failure and a legitimate empty review are no longer distinguishable: any caller that maps a findings-free RawReview to a pass/no-issues verdict will report a broken or truncated model response as a clean review. This is a public/exported path (`normalizeReview` is exported and has no other validation layer in the repo), so the unusable contract is the defect even with no in-repo caller today.

findings.title: Resolve PR head/base SHAs on workflow_dispatch before review
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted 'Resolve PR refs' step handled the non-pull_request event by calling `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json headRefOid/baseRefOid/baseRef` and feeding those SHAs to checkout and to PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA. The job is still explicitly runnable via `on: workflow_dispatch` (with a required `pr_number` input) and the job `if:` still permits it (line 24). On workflow_dispatch, `github.event.pull_request` is null, so the replacement fallbacks resolve to unrelated values: `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref }}` (line 29) checks out `github.ref` (the dispatched branch, normally the default branch) instead of the PR head, the base fetch (line 35) falls back to `main` instead of the PR's base ref, and `PR_BASE_SHA`/`PR_HEAD_SHA` (lines 45-46) become empty strings. Manual dispatches therefore review the wrong tree and hand the tool no diff base. The removed resolution was not replaced anywhere in the new steps.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch runs now use wrong ref and empty SHAs
findings.whyItBreaks: These values are read only from `github.event.pull_request.*`, but the workflow still declares `workflow_dispatch` with a required `pr_number` input (lines 10-14) and still routes it through `run: ... --pr ${{ github.event.inputs.pr_number || ... }}` (line 47). For a workflow_dispatch event the `pull_request` payload is absent, so `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` and `github.event.pull_request.base.sha` evaluate to empty strings -> PR_HEAD_SHA/PR_BASE_SHA are empty. The same fallback problem hits the checkout at line 29 (`github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref` -> `github.ref`, i.e. the dispatch branch, not the PR head) and the base fetch at line 35 (defaults to `main` instead of the PR's real base ref). The deleted `gh pr view ... headRefOid/baseRefOid/baseRef` step (base revision lines 27-45) existed precisely to resolve these for dispatch, so manual reviews now analyze the wrong commit with empty SHAs.

findings.title: Manual dispatch reviews default branch, not the requested PR
findings.whyItBreaks: On `workflow_dispatch` there is no `pull_request` payload, so `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` is empty and line 29's `ref:` falls back to `github.ref` — the ref the workflow was dispatched from (normally the default branch). The deleted `Resolve PR refs` step ran `gh pr view "$PR_NUM" --json headRefOid -q .headRefOid` for exactly this case, feeding the resolved SHA to both the checkout (old line 48) and `PR_HEAD_SHA`/`PR_BASE_SHA` (old lines 59-60). With it gone, lines 45-46 evaluate to empty on manual runs, and the CLI (`runGithub`) resolves `headSha = process.env.PR_HEAD_SHA || git rev-parse HEAD` and `baseSha = process.env.PR_BASE_SHA || git merge-base origin/main HEAD` — i.e. it diffs the default-branch checkout against itself (empty patch) and posts the review/check with `commit_id`/`head_sha` set to the default-branch tip. A manual `pr_number` dispatch therefore silently produces no review of PR #N and attaches its check to the wrong commit instead of the PR head.

findings.title: Restore maxBuffer on git() or large diffs fail with ENOBUFS
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1 MiB (1024*1024). The git() helper is used to capture the full unified diff (`git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"], cwd)`, src/adapters/local.ts:100) and the name-only list (line 101). For any PR whose patch output exceeds 1 MiB (common for large or generated diffs), spawnSync kills the child and sets res.error=ENOBUFS with res.status===null; the check `res.status !== 0` at line 12 then throws `git diff ... failed:` with an empty stderr, so the review cannot start. Previously the explicit `maxBuffer: 1024 * 1024 * 64` allowed 64 MiB patches. The sibling `gh()` helper still keeps that 64 MiB buffer (line 36), confirming the removal here is unintentional.

findings.title: Dropping git maxBuffer breaks review of diffs over 1 MiB
findings.whyItBreaks: git() is used by runLocal to capture the full patch via git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"], cwd) (src/adapters/local.ts:100). spawnSync's default maxBuffer is 1024*1024 bytes; when stdout exceeds it Node kills the child and sets res.error to ENOBUFS with res.status === null. The check at src/adapters/local.ts:12 then throws `git diff <sha> HEAD failed: ` (stderr is empty for ENOBUFS), so any PR whose diff exceeds ~1 MiB — common with lockfiles, generated code, or vendored assets — can no longer be reviewed at all, whereas the removed 64 MiB cap (still present on the sibling gh() helper at src/adapters/local.ts:33-36) previously handled them.

findings.title: Removing maxBuffer makes large git diffs abort the review
findings.whyItBreaks: The git() helper no longer passes maxBuffer, so spawnSync falls back to Node's default of 1024*1024 (1 MiB) for stdout. The very same helper is used to capture the whole patch at line 100 (`git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"], cwd)`); previously it was allowed 64 MiB. For any PR whose `git diff` output exceeds 1 MiB, spawnSync aborts the child with ENOBUFS, returning `status === null` (not 0) and truncated stdout, so the `res.status !== 0` check at line 12 throws `git diff ... failed: <stderr>` and `runLocal` aborts before review. Large PRs that were reviewable before this change now hard-fail with a misleading empty-stderr error. The `gh` helper at line 36 still carries the 64 MiB buffer, confirming the git side was the intended equivalent that got dropped.

findings.title: Error path downgraded to neutral check, no longer blocks merge
findings.whyItBreaks: In the catch block, the check-run conclusion was changed from "failure" to "neutral" (src/adapters/github.ts:191), while the summary still promises blocking behaviour: "Review errored and did NOT pass this PR." (src/adapters/github.ts:193). GitHub treats a check-run conclusion of neutral as successful for required status checks (same set as success/skipped), so when the review throws (e.g. a gh/git/API failure or model error) the "Needlefish" check now shows as passing instead of failing. A caller relying on this check as a merge gate can no longer distinguish "review failed to run" from the legitimate needs_human verdict (which also maps to neutral via VERDICT_CONCLUSION, src/adapters/github.ts:183), and the PR may be merged with no successful review. Previously the failure conclusion blocked the merge, so this is a real loss of the error signal on the live gating path.

findings.title: Review failure now posts neutral check, so errored review no longer blocks merge

findings.title: Review error path no longer fails the Needlefish check

findings.title: Restore severity normalization; lowercase/whitespace severities now become P3
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation computed `String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` before checking membership, so inputs like "p0", "P1 " or "p2" normalized to a valid severity. The new code feeds `raw.severity` straight into `SEVERITIES.includes(...)`, so any non-exact-case value ("p0", "p1") fails the check and falls through to the default, which was also changed from "P1" to "P3". Substituting real values: {severity:"p0"} -> base "P0" vs head "P3"; {severity: undefined} -> base "P1" vs head "P3". A critical finding reported in lowercase is therefore silently reclassified as the lowest severity, which can flip the review verdict toward pass. The base's explicit trim/toUpperCase is evidence that non-canonical case is a real input.

findings.title: Severity normalization removed; loose values silently downgrade to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: Base version computed `const sev = String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase()` and kept it if it matched SEVERITIES, else fell back to "P1". The new body tests `SEVERITIES.includes(raw.severity as Severity)` on the raw value with no trim/case-fold and falls back to "P3". Because the real entry point is `normalizeFinding(raw: Partial<Finding>)`, called from `normalizeReview(raw: any)` at src/shared/schema.ts:132 on parsed JSON/LLM output, values like "p0", "p1 ", or "P1\n" now fail the exact-match includes check and are classified P3 (least severe) instead of being normalized to their true class or at worst P1. A P0/P1 finding emitted in a case variant is silently delivered as P3, changing downstream triage/verdict ranking while still type-checking as Severity.

findings.title: Restore severity normalization; removing it downgrades P0/P1 to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding parses untrusted model output (normalizeReview maps raw.findings where raw is `any` @src/shared/schema.ts:132). Base normalized the field with String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase() before validating, so 'p0', 'P1 ', 'p2\n' all matched SEVERITIES and were honored. Head compares raw.severity verbatim, so those same values now fail SEVERITIES.includes(...) and are rewritten to 'P3' (lowest), and genuinely missing/non-string severities now default to 'P3' instead of 'P1'. Net effect: a critical finding emitted as 'p0' is silently downgraded two levels and an unparseable severity is reported as low-risk rather than as an unknown — the failure is conflated with a legitimate P3 value and is indistinguishable downstream.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token scrubbing before spawning codex
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed lines built a sanitized env ({ ...process.env } minus GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, GITHUB_API_TOKEN) and passed it via `env`. With `env` omitted, child_process.spawnSync defaults to the parent's full process.env, so the codex subprocess — and any repo content / model output / prompt-injection it processes while running against opts.repoPath — can read and exfiltrate those credentials. This reverses the prior token-scrubbing control that protected the parent's GitHub secrets.

findings.title: Re-enables leaking GH/GITHUB tokens into codex subprocess env
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff deletes the env-scrubbing block (`delete env.GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN`) and drops the `env` option from `spawnSync`. With no `env` passed, the child `codex exec` inherits `process.env` verbatim (Node default), so all three credentials are now present in the subprocess that runs inside the reviewed repo (`cwd: opts.repoPath`) with a read-only sandbox. codex exec runs agent-driven commands and can print/inspect its environment or make network calls, so a malicious or compromised change under review can read and exfiltrate the ambient GitHub token that the removed lines were explicitly there to withhold — an attacker-controlled PR can obtain a token whose privileges were never intended to be exposed to it.

findings.title: Restore GitHub token sanitization before spawning codex
findings.whyItBreaks: This hunk deletes `const env = { ...process.env }` plus `delete env.GH_TOKEN / GITHUB_TOKEN / GITHUB_API_TOKEN`, and also deletes the `env` option from the `spawnSync` call. As a result `spawnSync(bin, args, { cwd, input, encoding, timeout, maxBuffer })` falls back to inheriting the parent's full `process.env` (Node child_process default). The child is `codex exec` (`src/shared/codex.ts:20`), an autonomous agent that ingests the untrusted `prompt`/repo content and is not sandboxed against network access by `-s read-only` (read-only only restricts filesystem writes). Every GH/GitHub credential in the runner's environment is now visible to that child and can be read/exfiltrated by prompt-injected or tool-driven behavior — the exact exposure the removed lines existed to prevent. This regresses a previously safe behavior with no compensating benefit, and `runCodex` is an exported public surface, so the leak is the API contract itself regardless of in-repo callers.

findings.title: Removing fork guard runs untrusted fork code on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` restricted this job to same-repo branches. With it gone, the `pull_request` trigger now also fires the job for fork PRs. The job runs on a `self-hosted` runner (line 18), checks out the PR head SHA (line 23), runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (install/postinstall lifecycle scripts from the PR's package.json, line 28) and then executes the PR-authored `src/cli.ts` via tsx (line 34) with `GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}` (line 33). Any user who can open a fork PR can therefore run arbitrary attacker-controlled code on persistent self-hosted infrastructure, with whatever ambient credentials/network access that runner holds — the canonical GitHub Actions self-hosted-runner anti-pattern the removed guard existed to prevent.

findings.title: Restore fork guard; PR code now runs untrusted on self-hosted runner

The job still (a) checks out the PR head SHA (`actions/checkout` ref=${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}, line 20-24), (b) runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28, executes dependency/lifecycle scripts from the PR), and (c) runs `tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34, the PR's own source) on `runs-on: self-hosted` (line 18). A fork author therefore gets arbitrary code execution inside the self-hosted runner host (persistent workspace, cached credentials, network reach to internal services) merely by opening/synchronizing a PR. The guard existed precisely to prevent this and there is no other such predicate in the repo (git grep at base: only review.yml:19).

findings.title: Restore fork guard so self-hosted job never runs untrusted fork PR code

Deleting that line means a PR opened from a fork now runs on `runs-on: self-hosted`: the job checks out the attacker-controlled `github.event.pull_request.head.sha` (line 24) and runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 29) plus `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts` (line 34). Installing dependencies executes package lifecycle/postinstall scripts authored by the fork, giving untrusted code execution on Frank's persistent self-hosted runner (host filesystem, network/services, and cached artifacts from other jobs). For fork PRs GitHub downgrades GITHUB_TOKEN to read-only, so the checkout+install path — not the write scopes — is the exposed surface, and self-hosted runners are explicitly not safe for untrusted fork code.

findings.title: Env value 0 for runner kill timing is silently discarded
findings.whyItBreaks: The base guard `parsed >= 0` explicitly accepted 0 as a valid duration; the new `parsed > 0` rejects it and returns fallbackMs instead. The only consumers are the two module constants (RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS @src/shared/runner-process.ts:3, RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS @src/shared/runner-process.ts:7) read via setTimeout @src/shared/runner-process.ts:124 and :123. Substituting value "0": NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 -> `parsed > 0` rejects -> fallback 5000, so the hard-kill timer fires 5000ms after SIGTERM instead of immediately; NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 -> rejects -> fallback 2000, so finish(null,"SIGKILL") at :122 waits 2000ms instead of resolving at once. An operator who configured 0 (no grace / immediate escalation) gets a silently different, slower kill path with no warning anywhere, and the exported helper's behavior for a valid input is changed for all external callers too.

findings.title: Restore coverage backstop so large-PR review cannot skip changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge keeps only the top MAX_HOTSPOTS (=6, line 26/93) hotspots and previously appended a tail-coverage hotspot containing every changed file the map pass did not assign to a selected hotspot (base d03f12b lines 98-110, comment: 'never silently skip a changed file'). That block is deleted. Now any changed file not named in one of the 6 selected hotspots is never sent to a deep pass, and nothing records the omission (no checked entry, no residual risk), so the tool returns a PASS-shaped result for a PR whose files were never examined — exactly the silent coverage loss the removed comment guarded against.

findings.title: Stop discarding deep-pass residual_risks before the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: candidateMerged.residual_risks is now hardcoded to [] (line 113). In the base version each deep pass's residual risks were accumulated (`residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)`, base line 127) and forwarded as candidateMerged.residual_risks (base line 140), which is serialized into the critic prompt via `{{FINDINGS}}` (line 116). Deep reviewers emit residual_risks specifically for gaps they could not resolve, including entries with blocks:true that are meant to prevent a PASS. After this change those signals never reach the critic, so a blocking gap found while deep-reviewing a hotspot can no longer influence the verdict gate.

findings.title: Deep-pass blocking residual risks are discarded before the verdict
findings.whyItBreaks: Head hardcodes `residual_risks: []` in `candidateMerged` and deletes `residuals.push(...res.residual_risks)` (base src/core/review.ts:127,140). Each deep pass is explicitly instructed (prompts/deep.md:28,82) to record unresolved triggers as residual risks with `blocks:true`. Those records previously flowed into the critic via candidateMerged, and deriveVerdict maps ANY residual with blocks:true to "needs_human" (src/core/verdict.ts:11-12). With the signals dropped, the critic never sees them and the final verdict computed at src/core/review.ts:122 can now return "pass" where base returned "needs_human" — a false PASS on a real merge gate.

findings.title: Removed tail-coverage backstop silently skips changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Head computes `hotspots = sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (MAX_HOTSPOTS=6 at line 26) and deletes the base block that added a "tail-coverage" hotspot for every changed file not present in a selected hotspot (base src/core/review.ts:96-110, whose comment states 'never silently skip a changed file'). When the map pass returns more than MAX_HOTSPOTS surfaces (large PRs are exactly when reviewLarge runs) or omits a changed file, files outside the surviving hotspots are no longer deep-reviewed and produce no residual/blocks signal, yet a verdict is still emitted — a silent coverage loss that can yield a PASS over unreviewed changes.

findings.title: Critic prompt keeps literal {{BASE}}/{{HEAD}} placeholders
findings.whyItBreaks: Head removes `.replace("{{BASE}}", bundle.baseSha).replace("{{HEAD}}", bundle.headSha)` from the critic prompt in both reviewLarge (head lines 115-117) and reviewSmall (head lines 59-61), but critic.md still carries a '# Refs' section with `BASE: {{BASE}}` / `HEAD: {{HEAD}}` (prompts/critic.md:29-31) and tells the critic to re-open hunks with `git diff <base>..<head>`. The rendered prompt therefore contains the literal strings {{BASE}}/{{HEAD}}, so the critic can no longer run those commands and its core re-verification (per-finding hunks) is broken; weak findings it should have pruned can survive.

findings.title: Restore the changed-file coverage backstop in reviewLarge
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted tail-coverage hotspot was the only guarantee that every entry in bundle.changedFiles is deep-reviewed. After `sortByRisk(mapResult.hotspots).slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (line 93) the loop at line 97 deep-reviews at most 6 hotspots; any changed file not referenced by one of them — including files in hotspots dropped by the slice — is now never passed to deep.md, yields no finding and no residual_risks. deriveVerdict then has nothing blocking and can return a PASS for a large PR whose changed files were never examined. Previously those files were collected into a tail-coverage hotspot (comment: "never silently skip a changed file") and any deep failure recorded a blocks:true residual.

findings.title: Preserve deep-review residual and failure signals
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass still returns residual_risks (including blocks:true), but the loop no longer collects `res.residual_risks` and candidateMerged.residual_risks is hard-coded to `[]` (line 113). That array is serialized into the critic prompt at line 116 and is the uncertainty/blocking evidence the critic and deriveVerdict rely on to override a PASS, so a deep pass reporting an unresolvable or blocking risk can now silently yield a PASS. The same hunk removed the try/catch that recorded a blocks:true residual when a deep pass threw, so a single failing hotspot now aborts the whole reviewLarge instead of degrading with the other hotspots' findings preserved.

findings.title: Round seconds before carrying into minutes in formatDuration
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code computes minutes = Math.floor(ms / 60000) and seconds = Math.round((ms % 60000) / 1000) independently, so the rounded seconds can reach 60 without carrying into minutes. For ms = 119999: minutes = 1, remainder = 59999, 59999/1000 = 59.999, Math.round -> 60, yielding the invalid '1m 60s' (base produced '2m 0s'). For ms = 59999 it yields '60s'. Any ms whose ms % 60000 falls in [59500, 59999] hits this. Both call sites (render.ts:75 per-step durations, render.ts:80 total) render this text verbatim into the user-facing summary.

findings.title: formatDuration can render "Xm 60s" for sub-minute remainders
findings.whyItBreaks: minutes and seconds are rounded independently from ms, so the remainder can round up to 60: with ms=119999 minutes=floor(119999/60000)=1 and seconds=round((119999%60000)/1000)=round(59.999)=60, yielding "1m 60s"; ms=59999 yields "60s". The pre-change code rounded total seconds first (Math.round(ms/1000)) so the carry propagated, e.g. 119999 -> totalSeconds=120 -> minutes=2 -> "2m 0s". Either branch can now print an out-of-range seconds value, and this string is user-visible in the rendered stats line (formatDuration called at src/shared/render.ts:75 and :80).

findings.title: Round-up of seconds can emit invalid 60s component
findings.whyItBreaks: `seconds = Math.round((ms % 60000) / 1000)` can equal 60 while `minutes` was already floored from the truncated ms, so values within half a second below a minute boundary produce out-of-range output: ms=59_600 → "0m 60s", ms=60_000+59_600 → "1m 60s". The previous formula rounded total seconds first and took `totalSeconds % 60`, which always stayed in 0..59. Both callers at src/shared/render.ts:75 and src/shared/render.ts:80 print the string directly into the review summary, so the malformed duration is user-visible.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, contradicting its positive contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The body changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` now returns 0 instead of throwing. The unchanged carrier — the exported name `parsePositiveInteger` and the thrown message `"${label} requires a positive integer"` — promises a strictly positive (>0) result. 0 is not positive, so the exported validation contract is now false: a caller relying on the guaranteed strictly-positive return value (loop bounds, array/collection sizing, counts, timeouts) receives a value the contract said it would never return, and the promised validation no longer holds. Because it is an exported/public validator, the promise itself is the contract, and callers cannot know the function no longer enforces it.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0 despite positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported validator's name (`parsePositiveInteger`) and its unchanged error message `"${label} requires a positive integer"` promise rejection of any non-positive value, but the guard now reads `parsed < 0`, so `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` returns 0 instead of throwing. Zero satisfies Number.isInteger and is not < 0, so it slips through. The promise (validation) is what callers rely on, and the body no longer implements it: a caller using this to bound a count/timeout/retry or to reject a zero-sized or zero-valued parameter receives an out-of-contract 0 rather than an error. This is a regression from the previous `<= 0` behavior, which correctly rejected 0.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0, breaking positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard was loosened from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so the string "0" now passes and the function returns 0. The exported function's name (`parsePositiveInteger`) and its own thrown message (`${label} requires a positive integer`) both promise a strictly positive result, but the body now admits a non-positive value. Substitution: value=0 -> guard `parsed < 0` @src/shared/runner.ts:32 is false -> no throw -> returns 0. Before this diff, 0 -> `parsed <= 0` true -> threw. Any caller using this as the positive-integer validator for a size/timeout/count receives 0 where the contract guarantees >0, silently admitting an invalid configuration.
